title: Story Cut 01: Project Azorian (hook lab A/B/C; TikTok 80-110 s)
photo_source: Wikimedia Commons, CIA, USGS, NOAA (public domain)
_note: Story Cut (research/52): protagonist with a want, stacked loops, 4 escalation steps (cover story, claw, break mid-lift, press), payoff ~60%, false calm ~80% then the drop, ironic kicker. Hook lab: three myth groups that differ ONLY in the first beat (A scene, B proof, C challenge); every later line is identical so the opening is the only variable. Photos reuse the licence-checked Glomar set from cases-01 (Commons PD: CIA, US Government, USGS; Openverse NOAA PD). Gates: tools/story.py, openloop.py, coldopen.py. Render: episode.py scripts/story-01.json story-01 --skip-long, then rename short-azorian<V>.mp4 to story-azorian-<V>.mp4.

beats.bonus: Project Azorian (1974): the CIA's Hughes Glomar Explorer, sold to the world as Howard Hughes's deep-sea mining ship, lifted part of the sunken Soviet missile submarine K-129 from about 16,500 feet down. It cost about $800 million. Asked about the ship, the CIA would 'neither confirm nor deny', now called a Glomar response.
beats.caption: Project Azorian: the CIA's secret plan to steal a Soviet submarine. Did they get it? 🚢 all of it / 🧩 a piece / ❌ nothing #projectazorian #coldwar #cia #declassified #meatballinvestigates Follow Meatball for a new case every day 🍝
sources: Wikipedia, Project Azorian: 1974 CIA recovery of part of Soviet submarine K-129 from about 16,500 ft (5,000 m) with the Hughes Glomar Explorer; Howard Hughes's Summa Corporation fronted the ship as a deep-sea manganese-nodule mining venture; the capture vehicle (nicknamed Clementine) was lowered on a pipe string through the ship's moon pool in July-August 1974; part of the grapple failed during the lift and most of the section broke away; a forward section was recovered with the remains of six Soviet sailors, buried at sea with honors in September 1974 (filmed; the film was given to Russia in 1992); the Los Angeles Times broke the story in February 1975; total cost about US$800 million — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Azorian (checked 2026-10-26)

Wikipedia, Soviet submarine K-129 (1959): Golf II-class diesel-electric ballistic missile submarine, sank in the North Pacific in March 1968 with all 98 crew; carried three R-21 nuclear-armed ballistic missiles (plus nuclear torpedoes); the Soviet search failed; the US located it with SOSUS data and USS Halibut photographed the wreck — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_submarine_K-129_(1960)

Wikipedia, Glomar response: 'we can neither confirm nor deny', the CIA's answer to journalist Harriet Ann Phillippi's FOIA request about the Glomar Explorer (Phillippi v. CIA, D.C. Cir. 1976); the term is still used for such answers by US agencies and others today — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glomar_response
CIA, 'Project AZORIAN' (CIA Museum exhibit and declassified history, 2010) — https://www.cia.gov/legacy/museum/exhibit/project-azorian/

National Security Archive (George Washington University), 'Project Azorian: The CIA's Declassified History of the Glomar Explorer' (Electronic Briefing Book No. 305, 2010) — https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/nukevault/ebb305/

beats.say: The CIA wanted that sub. Howard Hughes put his name on the plan. Did they get it?
See, in 1968, a Soviet sub, K-129, sank with ninety-eight men.
It carried three nuclear missiles. And the Soviets couldn't find it.
The Americans could. A US spy sub photographed the wreck.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Problem: it was three miles down. So how do you grab it?

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Build a giant ship with a claw. But that ship needs a cover story.
Enter Howard Hughes. He said it was his ship, mining rocks off the sea floor.

shots.photo: Manganese nodule from the cover story (CIA)

beats.say: His name, on a spy ship. If it went wrong? I'd have fainted.
But this mining ship had a secret pool in its belly, hiding a claw.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: July 1974. They lowered the claw three miles. Then a Soviet ship showed up, and watched.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: The claw closed around the sub, and it started to rise.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Then, on the way up, part of the claw broke. Most of the sub fell back.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery
CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: But they got a piece. A chunk of a Soviet nuclear sub, stolen.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: And inside? Six Soviet sailors, buried at sea with honors.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Follow Meatball Investigates. Case files every day.
The ship sailed home. The cover held. Everything was fine.
Except, just before it sailed, thieves had robbed Hughes's company office in Los Angeles.
They took secret papers. One tied Hughes to the CIA.
The CIA called the FBI. The FBI called the police. By 1975, it was in the papers.
A reporter asked the CIA about the ship.
The answer? We can neither confirm nor deny.
That non-answer is named after the fake ship: a Glomar response. Governments still use it today.
This is the real ship the CIA built to steal a Soviet submarine.
